biology.animal-kingdom.name: Biological Classification
biology.animal-kingdom.subject: Biology
biology.animal-kingdom.why: Animal Kingdom is a major taxonomic grouping built upon the principles of biological classification.

check.q: Which of the following is the correct hierarchical sequence in biological classification from broad to specific?
check.explain: Classification moves from broader categories like Kingdom and Phylum down to specific ones like Class and Order.

biology.animal-kingdom.name: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
biology.animal-kingdom.subject: Science
biology.animal-kingdom.idea: Basis of animal and plant diversity
biology.animal-kingdom.why: Provides the foundational understanding of how organisms are grouped based on shared characteristics.

check.q: What is the primary basis for classifying organisms into major groups?
options: Fundamental similarities in design and characteristics
check.explain: Organisms are classified based on fundamental similarities in their body design and characteristics.

biology.animal-kingdom.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life
biology.animal-kingdom.subject: Science
biology.animal-kingdom.idea: Basic cellular organization and tissue types
biology.animal-kingdom.why: Animal classification heavily relies on cellular levels of organization, tissue layers, and body plans.

check.q: Which organelle is present in plant cells but absent in animal cells?
check.explain: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the cell membrane, whereas animal cells do not.

biology.biomolecules.name: Cell: The Unit of Life
biology.biomolecules.subject: Biology
biology.biomolecules.idea: Cellular structural components and chemical composition
biology.biomolecules.why: Biomolecules are the organic and inorganic molecules that build up cellular structures and drive metabolic pathways.

check.q: Which cellular organelle is primarily responsible for packaging proteins?
check.explain: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins into vesicles for transport.

biology.biomolecules.name: Carbon and its Compounds
biology.biomolecules.subject: Science
biology.biomolecules.idea: Covalent bonding and functional groups in carbon compounds
biology.biomolecules.why: Biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids are complex carbon-based macromolecules containing various functional groups.

check.q: What type of bond is formed between carbon atoms in organic molecules?
check.explain: Carbon atoms share electrons to form strong covalent bonds.

biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life
biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.subject: Science
biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.idea: Basic cell structure and organelle functions
biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.why: Cell: The Unit of Life builds directly upon foundational knowledge of cell organelles, plasma membrane, and cytoplasm learned previously.

check.q: Which cell organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
check.explain: Mitochondria generate most of the chemical energy needed to power the cell's biochemical reactions.

biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.name: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.subject: Science
biology.cell-the-unit-of-life.why: Understanding how cells were discovered and viewed requires familiarity with microscopic life and magnification concepts.

check.q: Which instrument is essential for observing microscopic cells and microorganisms?
check.explain: A microscope magnifies objects that are too small to be seen with the naked eye.

biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.name: Principles of Inheritance and Variation
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.subject: Biology
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.idea: Mendelian inheritance and chromosomal basis of traits
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.why: Molecular basis of inheritance explains the physical and chemical nature of the genes studied in Mendelian genetics.

check.q: If a plant with genotype Tt is crossed with tt, what fraction of offspring will be tt?
check.explain: A test cross between Tt and tt yields 50% Tt and 50% tt.

biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.name: Heredity
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.subject: Science
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.idea: DNA as the hereditary material and genes
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.why: It introduces chromosomes, DNA, and the basic concept that genes control traits before molecular details are studied.

check.q: Which component of a cell contains information for inheritance of traits?
check.explain: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) in the cell nucleus is the carrier of hereditary information.

biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.subject: Science
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.idea: Cellular organelles like the nucleus and chromosomes
biology.molecular-basis-of-inheritance.why: Genetic material (DNA and RNA) resides inside the nucleus and cellular structures, which must be understood first.

check.q: Which cell organelle is known as the control center of the cell and houses genetic material?
check.explain: The nucleus contains the chromosomes made of DNA which control cellular activities.

biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.name: Heredity
biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.subject: Science
biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.idea: Mendelian inheritance and basic monohybrid crosses
biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.why: Principles of Inheritance and Variation builds directly upon basic Mendelian crosses, allele segregation, and phenotypic ratios.

check.q: What is the phenotypic ratio in the $F_2$ generation of a Mendelian monohybrid cross?
check.explain: A monohybrid cross yields 3 dominant to 1 recessive phenotype in the F2 generation.

biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.name: Reproduction: How Life Continues
biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.subject: Science
biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.idea: Basic concept of trait transmission from parents to offspring
biology.principles-of-inheritance-and-va.why: Understanding inheritance requires knowing that offspring inherit traits from both parents through reproduction.

check.q: What primarily ensures continuity of life and transmission of traits between generations?
check.explain: Reproduction is the fundamental biological process by which living organisms pass on their traits to offspring.

biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.name: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.subject: Biology
biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.idea: Meiosis produces haploid gametes for sexual reproduction
biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.why: Microspores and megaspores in flowering plants form through meiotic divisions.

check.q: If a diploid plant cell has $24$ chromosomes, how many chromosomes will each cell have after meiosis?
check.explain: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, producing haploid cells with $n = 12$.

biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.name: How do Organisms Reproduce?
biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.subject: Science
biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.idea: Basic structure of flowers and sexual reproduction
biology.sexual-reproduction-in-flowering.why: It introduces stamen, carpel, pollination, and fertilization as the foundations for angiosperm reproduction.

check.q: Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?
check.explain: The anther is the part of the stamen that produces and stores pollen grains.

chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.name: Atomic Structure
chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.subject: Chemistry
chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.why: Chemical bonding depends on how valence electrons are shared, gained, or lost between atoms.

check.q: What is the number of valence electrons in a neutral Nitrogen atom (atomic number 7)?
check.explain: Nitrogen has an electronic configuration of 2, 5, meaning it has 5 valence electrons in its outermost shell.

chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.name: Metals and Non-metals
chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.subject: Science
chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.why: Provides the foundational understanding of electrovalent bonds formed between metals and non-metals.

check.q: Which type of bond is typically formed when a metal reacts with a non-metal by transferring electrons?
check.explain: Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them, forming oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic forces in an ionic bond.

chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.name: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.subject: Science
chemistry.chemical-bonding-and-molecular.why: Molecules and compounds are formed when atoms combine through chemical bonds, a concept rooted here.

check.q: Which of the following represents a chemical compound rather than an element?
check.explain: Water is made of two different elements (hydrogen and oxygen) chemically combined, whereas the others are pure elements.

chemistry.coordination-compounds.name: d- and f-Block Elements
chemistry.coordination-compounds.subject: Chemistry
chemistry.coordination-compounds.idea: d-orbital electronic configurations and transition metal properties
chemistry.coordination-compounds.why: Coordination compounds centrally involve transition metal ions with partially filled d-orbitals interacting with ligands.

check.q: What is the general valence shell electronic configuration of transition metals?
check.explain: Transition metals fill the $(n-1)d$ orbitals after the $ns$ orbital is partially or fully filled.

chemistry.coordination-compounds.name: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure
chemistry.coordination-compounds.subject: Chemistry
chemistry.coordination-compounds.idea: Coordinate covalent bonding and molecular orbital overlap
chemistry.coordination-compounds.why: Ligands donate electron pairs to the central metal atom via coordinate bonds, explained by bonding theories.

check.q: Which type of bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons to the shared pair?
check.explain: A coordinate covalent bond (dative bond) involves a pair of electrons donated entirely by a single atom.

chemistry.coordination-compounds.name: Acids, Bases and Salts
chemistry.coordination-compounds.subject: Science
chemistry.coordination-compounds.idea: Lewis acid-base concepts involving electron pairs
chemistry.coordination-compounds.why: Central metal ions act as Lewis acids and ligands act as Lewis bases in forming coordination complexes.

check.q: According to the Lewis definition, what is a base?
check.explain: A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor, which precisely describes ligands in coordination chemistry.

chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.name: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure
chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.subject: Chemistry
chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.idea: Lewis structures, hybridization, and molecular geometry
chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.why: General Organic Chemistry requires drawing structures, identifying hybridization, and understanding bond shapes.

check.q: What is the hybridization of the central carbon atom in methane ($CH_4$)?
check.explain: Carbon in methane forms four single sigma bonds, corresponding to sp^3 hybridization.

chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.name: Carbon and its Compounds
chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.subject: Science
chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.idea: Covalent bonding and basic carbon chain structures
chemistry.general-organic-chemistry.why: Provides the foundational vocabulary of carbon skeletons and functional groups needed before studying electronic effects.

check.q: Which functional group is present in ethanol ($CH_3CH_2OH$)?
check.explain: The -OH group attached to a carbon chain defines an alcohol.

mathematics.conic-sections.name: Straight Lines
mathematics.conic-sections.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.conic-sections.idea: Equation of a line and slope concepts
mathematics.conic-sections.why: Conic sections involve tangents, normals, and chords whose equations rely on straight line principles.

check.q: What is the slope of the line passing through $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 6)$?

mathematics.conic-sections.name: Coordinate Geometry
mathematics.conic-sections.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.conic-sections.idea: Distance formula between two points in a plane
mathematics.conic-sections.why: The definition of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas is based on distances between points and lines/foci.

check.q: What is the distance between the points $(0, 0)$ and $(3, 4)$?
check.explain: Using the distance formula, $\sqrt{(3-0)^2 + (4-0)^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

mathematics.conic-sections.name: Quadratic Equations
mathematics.conic-sections.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.conic-sections.idea: Solving quadratic equations and finding roots
mathematics.conic-sections.why: Finding intersections of lines and conics or determining standard forms requires solving quadratic equations.

check.q: What are the roots of the equation $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$?
check.explain: Factoring gives $(x-2)(x-3) = 0$, so the roots are $2$ and $3$.

mathematics.integral-calculus.name: Limits, Continuity & Differentiability
mathematics.integral-calculus.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.integral-calculus.idea: Defining derivatives as limits of difference quotients
mathematics.integral-calculus.why: Integral calculus relies on the fundamental theorem of calculus, connecting integration directly to differentiation.

check.q: What is the derivative of $f(x) = x^2$ using limits?
check.explain: The limit of $((x+h)^2 - x^2)/h$ as $h \to 0$ simplifies to $2x$.

mathematics.integral-calculus.name: Polynomials
mathematics.integral-calculus.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.integral-calculus.idea: Power rule for algebraic polynomial expressions
mathematics.integral-calculus.why: Integration heavily relies on reversing the power rule for polynomials to find antiderivatives.

check.q: What is the expanded form of $(x + 1)(x + 2)?$
check.explain: Multiplying gives $x^2 + 2x + x + 2 = x^2 + 3x + 2$.

mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.name: Sets, Relations & Functions
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.why: Limits and continuity fundamentally describe the behavior of functions as inputs approach a value.

check.q: Which of the following defines a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$?
options: Every input has at most one output
Every output must have an input
Every input has infinitely many outputs
The graph can intersect a vertical line twice
check.explain: A function associates each element in the domain with exactly one element in the codomain.

mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.name: Real Numbers
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.idea: Concept of real numbers and inequalities
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.why: Limits require understanding arbitrarily small distances and neighborhoods on the real number line.

check.q: Which real number satisfies the inequality $|x - 2| < 0.1$?
check.explain: Distance from $2$ must be less than $0.1$, so $1.9 < x < 2.1$. Only $2.05$ falls in this range.

mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.name: Introduction to Linear Polynomials
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.idea: Behavior of linear expressions near points
mathematics.limits-continuity-and-differ.why: Understanding linear trends helps grasp how values change continuously around a point.

check.q: As $x$ gets closer and closer to $3$, what value does the expression $2x + 1$ approach?
check.explain: Substituting $x = 3$ directly into the continuous polynomial gives $2(3) + 1 = 7$.

mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.idea: Solving simultaneous linear equations using algebraic elimination
mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.why: Matrices are primarily used to represent and solve systems of linear equations.

check.q: What is the solution for $x$ in the system: $x + y = 5$ and $x - y = 1$?
check.explain: Adding both equations gives $2x = 6$, so $x = 3$.

mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.name: Operations with Integers
mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.idea: Performing arithmetic operations with positive and negative numbers
mathematics.matrices-and-determinants.why: Matrix addition, multiplication, and determinant calculations involve extensive signed number arithmetic.

check.q: What is the result of $(-3) \times (-4) + (-5)?$

mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.name: Straight Lines
mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.why: Three dimensional geometry extends straight line concepts to three dimensions using direction cosines and ratios.

check.q: What is the slope of a line passing through $(2, 3)$ and $(4, 7)$?

mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.name: Coordinate Geometry
mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.why: 3D geometry relies directly on the distance formula extended to three axes to find lengths and spheres.

check.q: What is the distance between the points $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$ in the coordinate plane?

mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.name: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.three-dimensional-geometry.why: Understanding 2D Cartesian coordinates is the foundational step before adding a third z-axis for 3D space.

check.q: In which quadrant does the point $(-3, 4)$ lie?
check.explain: Negative x-coordinate and positive y-coordinate place the point in the second quadrant.

physics.current-electricity.name: Electricity
physics.current-electricity.subject: Science
physics.current-electricity.idea: Ohm's law and basic circuit connections
physics.current-electricity.why: Current electricity builds directly on Ohm's law and series-parallel resistor combinations.

check.q: What is the current through a $6\,\Omega$ resistor connected across a $12\,\text{V}$ battery?
check.explain: Using Ohm's law, $I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\,\text{A}$.

physics.current-electricity.name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
physics.current-electricity.subject: Mathematics
physics.current-electricity.why: Complex resistive circuits and Kirchhoff's laws require solving systems of simultaneous linear equations.

check.q: If $x + y = 5$ and $x - y = 1$, what is the value of $x$?
check.explain: Adding both equations gives $2x = 6$, so $x = 3$.

physics.electrostatics.name: Electricity
physics.electrostatics.subject: Science
physics.electrostatics.idea: Electric charge, current, and potential difference
physics.electrostatics.why: Electrostatics studies charges at rest, building directly on the fundamental concept of electric charge and potential.

check.q: What is the SI unit of electric potential difference?
check.explain: Electric potential difference is measured in volts (V).

physics.electrostatics.name: Exploring Forces
physics.electrostatics.subject: Science
physics.electrostatics.idea: Non-contact forces like electrostatic and magnetic forces
physics.electrostatics.why: Coulomb's law in electrostatics describes the non-contact force between stationary electric charges.

check.q: Which of the following is an example of a non-contact force?
check.explain: Electrostatic force acts between charges without physical contact.

physics.kinematics.name: Describing Motion Around Us
physics.kinematics.subject: Science
physics.kinematics.idea: Defining speed, velocity, and acceleration vectors
physics.kinematics.why: Kinematics builds directly on these foundational concepts of motion.

check.q: What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent?
check.explain: Speed is defined as the rate of change of distance, given by the slope of a distance-time graph.

physics.kinematics.name: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates
physics.kinematics.subject: Mathematics
physics.kinematics.idea: Plotting points and tracking coordinates on a grid
physics.kinematics.why: Motion along a straight line or in a plane requires coordinate systems.

check.q: What are the coordinates of the origin on a standard 2D Cartesian plane?
check.explain: The origin is the reference point where both the x and y axes intersect, denoted as (0, 0).

physics.kinematics.name: Operations with Integers
physics.kinematics.subject: Mathematics
physics.kinematics.idea: Adding and subtracting positive and negative numbers
physics.kinematics.why: Kinematics requires handling directions and negative signs for displacement and velocity.

check.q: What is $-5 + 3$?
check.explain: Combining a negative number with a smaller positive number results in a negative difference: $-5 + 3 = -2$.

physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.name: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.subject: Science
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.idea: Magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.why: Provides the foundational qualitative understanding of Oersted's experiment and field lines needed before advanced calculations.

check.q: According to the right-hand thumb rule, if current flows upwards in a straight wire, the magnetic field lines around it are:
options: Straight lines parallel to the wire
check.explain: Curling the fingers of the right hand with the thumb pointing up gives a counter-clockwise direction.

physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.name: Electricity
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.subject: Science
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.idea: Electric current and potential difference basics
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.why: Defines current ($I$), which is the source of the magnetic fields studied in electromagnetism.

check.q: If a charge of 120 C passes through a conductor in 2 minutes, what is the current?
check.explain: Current $I = Q / t = 120\text{ C} / 120\text{ s} = 1\text{ A}$.

physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.name: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.subject: Science
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.idea: Basic attraction and repulsion of magnets
physics.magnetic-effects-of-current-and-.why: Introduces poles, magnetic materials, and basic magnetic forces built upon in magnetism.

check.q: What happens when the North pole of one magnet is brought near the North pole of another?
check.explain: Like magnetic poles repel each other, while unlike poles attract.

physics.oscillations-and-waves.name: Work, Energy & Power
physics.oscillations-and-waves.subject: Physics
physics.oscillations-and-waves.idea: Potential energy curves and stable equilibrium
physics.oscillations-and-waves.why: Used to analyze restoring forces and energy conservation in simple harmonic motion.

check.q: At a point of stable equilibrium for a conservative force, potential energy is at a:
check.explain: Stable equilibrium corresponds to a local minimum of potential energy where the restoring force points back.

physics.oscillations-and-waves.name: Introduction to Trigonometry
physics.oscillations-and-waves.subject: Mathematics
physics.oscillations-and-waves.idea: Sine and cosine functions of angles
physics.oscillations-and-waves.why: Required to express displacement, velocity, and phase relationships in harmonic waves and oscillations.

check.q: What is the value of $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \theta\right)$?
check.explain: By trigonometric identity, $\sin(\pi/2 + \theta) = \cos\theta$.

physics.ray-and-wave-optics.name: Light — Reflection and Refraction
physics.ray-and-wave-optics.subject: Science
physics.ray-and-wave-optics.idea: Laws of reflection and refraction Snell's law
physics.ray-and-wave-optics.why: Ray optics relies directly on Snell's law and ray tracing for mirrors and lenses.

check.q: If the angle of incidence in a medium is $30^\circ$ and the angle of refraction is $60^\circ$, what is the relative refractive index $\mu_{21}$?
check.explain: Snell's law gives $\mu_{21} = \frac{\sin 30^\circ}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, wait, $\mu_{21} = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Let's check options: $\sqrt{3}$ means $\sin 60 / \sin 30$. Correct index is 0.

physics.ray-and-wave-optics.name: Introduction to Trigonometry
physics.ray-and-wave-optics.subject: Mathematics
physics.ray-and-wave-optics.why: Deriving lens maker's formula and prism formulas requires trigonometric approximations and identities.

check.q: What is the value of $\sin(90^\circ - \theta)$?
check.explain: Standard complementary angle identity in right-angled triangles.

physics.rotational-motion.name: Kinematics
physics.rotational-motion.subject: Physics
physics.rotational-motion.idea: Resolving a vector into perpendicular components
physics.rotational-motion.why: Torque uses only the part of the force perpendicular to the arm, F sin θ, so τ = rF sin θ.

check.q: A 10 N force acts at $30^\circ$ to the x-axis. What is its component along the y-axis?
check.explain: $F_y = F\sin 30^\circ = 10 \times \tfrac{1}{2}$ = 5 N

physics.rotational-motion.name: Trigonometry
physics.rotational-motion.subject: Mathematics
physics.rotational-motion.idea: Values of sin and cos at standard angles
physics.rotational-motion.why: Every torque and component question needs sin 30°, cos 30° and friends without a calculator.

check.q: What is $\sin 30^\circ + \cos 60^\circ$?
check.explain: $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so the sum = 1

physics.rotational-motion.name: Introduction to Trigonometry
physics.rotational-motion.subject: Mathematics
physics.rotational-motion.why: Knowing which side is sin θ and which is cos θ decides F sin θ versus F cos θ.

check.q: In a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$, how long is the side opposite $\theta$?
check.explain: Opposite $= 10 \times \sin 30^\circ$ = 5

physics.semiconductor-electronics.name: Current Electricity
physics.semiconductor-electronics.subject: Physics
physics.semiconductor-electronics.idea: Ohm's law and electrical resistance in materials
physics.semiconductor-electronics.why: Semiconductor devices like diodes and transistors manipulate current-voltage characteristics governed by resistance.

check.q: A resistor has a potential difference of $12\text{ V}$ across it and a current of $2\text{ A}$ flowing through it. What is its resistance?
check.explain: Resistance $R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{12}{2} = 6 \; \Omega$.

physics.semiconductor-electronics.name: Atoms & Nuclei
physics.semiconductor-electronics.subject: Physics
physics.semiconductor-electronics.idea: Atomic energy levels and electron energy bands
physics.semiconductor-electronics.why: Conduction in semiconductors is explained via valence and conduction bands formed by overlapping atomic energy levels.

check.q: What primarily determines whether a solid is a conductor, semiconductor, or insulator?
options: The spacing between its energy bands
check.explain: The size of the forbidden energy gap (band gap) between valence and conduction bands dictates electrical behavior.

physics.semiconductor-electronics.name: Journey Inside the Atom
physics.semiconductor-electronics.subject: Science
physics.semiconductor-electronics.idea: Atomic structure, protons, electrons, and valence shell
physics.semiconductor-electronics.why: Semiconductors like silicon and germanium rely on covalent bonding and valence electrons for doping and charge carriers.

check.q: How many valence electrons does a silicon atom have in its outermost shell?
check.explain: Silicon has an atomic number of 14, with electronic configuration $2, 8, 4$, meaning it has 4 valence electrons.
